analysis.one_liner: Requires warehouse employers to disclose productivity quotas, provide paid rest breaks, and limit workplace surveillance and retaliation.
analysis.headline: The bill won 50 cosponsors, including 3 Republicans, but never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have given warehouse workers written notice of the productivity quotas and electronic monitoring they are subject to, barred quotas that cut into legally required breaks or bathroom time, and guaranteed a paid 15-minute rest break for every 4 hours worked. It would let workers and their union or advocate see their own speed data, dispute inaccurate records, and take quota-related claims to court instead of forced arbitration. It would also direct OSHA to write the first national ergonomics standard for warehouses and speed up the fixing of serious safety violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Warehouse, distribution-center, and courier workers who are tracked against productivity quotas — a workforce that is heavily hourly, often immigrant, and disproportionately without a union. They would gain: written quota disclosures in their own language, paid rest breaks, the right to see and dispute the speed data used to judge or fire them, protection from retaliation with a presumption favoring the worker, freedom from forced arbitration on these claims, and eventual OSHA ergonomics and medical-referral standards. Unions and worker advocacy groups would also gain formal roles in inspections, complaints, and a new quota task force.

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to give each quota-covered worker a written description of every quota, the discipline that can follow missing it, and exactly what surveillance data is collected, how, and by whom — with 2 business days' notice before any change.

Bans quotas that interfere with legally required meal and rest breaks, bathroom use with reasonable travel time, health and safety rules, or accommodations, and bars firing or disciplining a worker based solely on rankings against other workers or on second-by-second tallies of off-task time.
Guarantees one 15-minute paid rest break for every 4 hours worked, with notices and signs in English, Spanish, and each worker's primary language.

Gives workers — or a union or worker advocacy group they designate — the right to request their own work speed data and aggregated data for comparable coworkers in a readable format within 7 business days, to have inaccurate data corrected, and to have discipline based on bad data reviewed and adjusted.

Makes retaliation within 90 days of a protected activity a rebuttable presumption against the employer, voids forced arbitration agreements for these claims, eases class-action certification, and sets civil penalties up to $76,987 per violation and $769,870 for willful or repeat violations.

Requires the Labor Department to open an investigation — with an on-site inspection and a worker-designated observer present — at any warehouse facility with an injury rate 1.5 times the industry average, or after 5 credible complaints at one site or 10 across multiple sites.

Directs OSHA to issue a national ergonomics standard within 4 years and a standard ensuring prompt first aid and medical referral within 3 years, and requires serious, willful, or repeated safety violations to be corrected while the employer contests them rather than after.
Adds quota misuse as an unfair labor practice under the National Labor Relations Act, so a quota used to suppress organizing rights is itself illegal.

analysis.who_pays: Warehouse and fulfillment operators — including retailers' distribution centers, wholesalers, courier and express delivery services, and the staffing agencies that supply their labor. They would bear the cost of written disclosures, recordkeeping, mandatory paid breaks, on-site first-aid and occupational-medicine arrangements, and civil penalties up to $76,987 per violation (up to $769,870 for willful or repeat violations), plus the loss of the current practice of using undisclosed, algorithm-set quotas and constant productivity tracking to manage the workforce. Some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers through prices or slower delivery; a share would come out of industry margins.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would land not only on giant fulfillment centers but on all businesses in five broad industry codes — including ordinary wholesalers and couriers — and would likely be passed to consumers through prices or slower fulfillment.

Employers would have to give written notice before almost any termination (with an exception only for egregious misconduct) and would face a presumption of illegal retaliation for any adverse action within 90 days of a protected activity, which raises the cost and risk of routine discipline in an at-will employment system.

The bill stacks several new enforcement regimes at once — a new Labor Department office, automatic investigations, OSHA rulemakings on 3-year deadlines, and a special class-action carve-out — and authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' through 2035, an open-ended appropriation.

Requiring correction of serious safety violations while an employer is still contesting the citation shifts the timeline toward the regulator; an employer later found not to have violated the law would still have spent the money fixing a non-existent violation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but targeted: they fall on a specific, highly profitable logistics sector rather than on workers, and the bill preserves state laws and union contracts that are more generous rather than overriding them. The main design risk is breadth — sweeping ordinary wholesalers and couriers into the same regime as industrial-scale fulfillment centers — and the combination of written-termination notices, a 90-day retaliation presumption, and very large per-violation penalties gives employers reason to fight it hard and to automate or offshore whatever they can. On balance it is a substantial transfer of information and bargaining power to workers at a meaningful but ordinary compliance cost to employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never held a hearing or markup, so the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross (D-NJ) introduced the Warehouse Worker Protection Act on June 5, 2024, with 24 original cosponsors from both parties listed on the bill.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction, which is the last action recorded for it.
Cosponsorship grew to 50 members — 47 Democrats and 3 Republicans — but the committee never scheduled a markup, and no floor vote was ever held before the 118th Congress expired.
Because the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill is dead and would need to be reintroduced from scratch in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large warehouse, e-commerce fulfillment, and courier operators are better off: no quota-disclosure rules, paid-break mandate, data-access rights, or OSHA ergonomics standard was ever enacted, and the status quo of undisclosed algorithmic quotas and productivity surveillance continues.

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote was ever held; among the 50 cosponsors, 47 were Democrats and only 3 were Republicans, so support was heavily Democratic with a small Republican minority.

industries.industry: Warehousing and e-commerce fulfillment (distribution centers, retailers' logistics arms, third-party logistics)
industries.note: The bill's main target: it would end the practice of managing workers through undisclosed, algorithm-set quotas and constant productivity tracking, force disclosure of quotas and surveillance, mandate paid rest breaks, and expose operators to penalties up to $76,987 per violation. The industry's interest in this bill runs directly against the workers it employs.
Covered under NAICS 492110, so parcel and delivery firms would face the same quota-disclosure, break, and penalty regime as warehouse operators.

industries.industry: Labor staffing agencies and employee-leasing firms
industries.note: The bill explicitly counts staffing agencies, temporary firms, and leasing entities as covered employers, closing the common route of shifting quota pressure onto a subcontracted workforce.

industries.industry: Workplace surveillance and productivity-tracking technology vendors
industries.note: Employers would have to disclose which vendor tracks workers, what data is collected and where it is stored and sold, and could collect only what is strictly necessary to monitor quota compliance — shrinking the market for worker-tracking products in warehouses.

industries.industry: Labor unions and worker advocacy organizations
industries.note: They could file and pursue complaints for workers without union membership, accompany federal inspectors, and sit on a new quota task force — a formal enforcement role they do not currently have in these workplaces.
